Q: Why is my SIMD implementation of octal string parsing unable to beat the compiler's? A:

I ran a benchmark to evaluate the performance of the two methods.

Please post the code of the benchmarks. Writing a benchmark for C/C++ can be a challenging task since the optimizer can over-optimize the code under test and remove a large part of the tested code.

So beware of this issue and provide your benchmarks. It may turn out that your implementation is faster and the benchmark was misleading because of over-optimization.
It would be best if you could use this site: https://quick-bench.com/ (sadly I was unable to force this site to compile your SIMD implementation).

Nitpicking: This function name parseOctalToBase10 is funny. It should be just parseOctal, since you are returning the actual value as represented in base 2 by hardware - there is no base 10 in this code. The conversion to base 10 happens when you convert this value back to a string.

Q: Compile only if .pyc is out-of-date? A:

what results are you getting? Because Python's default heuristics for compiling a PYC file already do that: the file is just rebuilt if it is out of date. Morever, this is somewhat complex - one can replicate the behavior, but ideally, to face all edge cases, you'd have to keep track of the source-code hash, current environment Python version and architecture, etc... all of that is built-into the import mechanism of the language.

The exception is the main Python file you call: so if instead of a package you have a lot of your application in a single big ".py" file you call directly with "python myapp.py" - that one is recompiled every time.

So - going to your question - the problem is that you are explicitly compiling your file- if you just import it, and call a function inside it that works as entry-point, instead of going through exec, you will benefit from the heuristic above.

import Child

Child.entry()

And inside Child.py, rearrange the code so that it won't run code on the top level of the module, and rather when a function is called - and then write this entry function to run that code:

Child.py - before

my()
spread_Apart()
with_side_effects_on_toplevel()
code()

to: Child.py - after:

def entry():
   my()
   spread_Apart()
   with_side_effects_on_toplevel()
   code()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # this if guard ensures the previous behavior is unchanged
    # when the file is called directly from CLI
    entry()

Q: Combining type predicate with assertion function A:

This is the subject of microsoft/TypeScript#60904 which was classified as "Not A Defect", meaning it is not considered a bug, but at most a missing feature.

You're trying to combine

  • control flow analysis of aliased conditions as implemented in microsoft/TypeScript#44730, with
  • assertion functions as implemented in microsoft/TypeScript#32695.

But this doesn't work for assertion predicates like asserts b is true. Such assertion predicates only act on the value b itself and does not behave identically to the control flow analysis that happens if you were to check b directly. See the implementer's comment. So when you write assertIsTrue(isValid) it ends up narrowing isValid to true without triggering narrowing of the condition isValid aliases.

As a workaround, instead of asserts b is true, you can use asserts b, which does behave identically to the control flow analysis when you check b directly for truthiness. It's not always possible to refactor predicates this way, but since the only way for a boolean b to be truthy is for it to be true, it suffices:

declare function assertIsTrue(b: boolean): asserts b;

function f(s: unknown): string {
  const isValid = test(s);
  assertIsTrue(isValid);  
  return s; // okay
}

One could potentially file a feature request to allow asserts x is true or asserts x is false to work as you expect for situations where x is an aliased condition, but expanding the behavior of control flow analysis is a potentially expensive operation. If a piece of code that didn't use to trigger more analysis now does so, that analysis could trigger further analysis, et cetera. So even if it might be useful to have extra analysis, it's not always feasible or worthwhile. This doesn't mean one should not file such a request, just that I wouldn't expect it to be implemented unless it obviously "pays for itself" in terms of complexity and performance.

Q: NoSQL graph database for AI A:

The requirements you're describing — stable user-defined IDs, mutable edge endpoints, atomic ops, balanced R/W — basically rule out most dedicated graph DBs.

ArangoDB is the closest fit. Edges are documents with a _key you control, you can update _from/_to freely, and it has proper transactions with atomic operations. Worth benchmarking for your write volume.

OrientDB (now Apache TinkerPop compatible) assigns persistent RIDs that never change. Edge mutation works, concurrency is decent — just test it under write contention before committing.

If traversal logic lives in your app anyway, plain Redis is honestly hard to beat: you own the ID scheme, INCR/WATCH/MULTI give you the atomics, and latency for mixed workloads is low. You lose native graph queries but gain control.

On Neo4j: its internal IDs are stable, the problem is you can't define your own key namespace independent of the internal ID space. Storing a UUID property and indexing it is a workaround, but edge immutability is a real blocker if you need it.

What's the graph density like? That'd help narrow it down.

Q: Print capture groups for every match A:

Replace for to while

... | perl -Mv5.14 -wne'say "$1-->$2" while /(\d)([a-z])/g'

With the for loop the regex is computed in a list context causing very different behavior

In particular, this is about the behavior of /g modifier in list-vs-scalar context. From perlop

The /g modifier specifies global pattern matching--that is, matching as many times as possible within the string. How it behaves depends on the context. In list context, it returns a list of the substrings matched by any capturing parentheses in the regular expression. If there are no parentheses, it returns a list of all the matched strings, as if there were parentheses around the whole pattern.

In scalar context, each execution of m//g finds the next match, returning true if it matches, and false if there is no further match. The position after the last match can be read or set using the pos() function; see "pos" in perlfunc. A failed match normally resets the search position to the beginning of the string, but you can avoid that by adding the /c modifier (for example, m//gc). Modifying the target string also resets the search position.

In the for loop's list the regex is in list context and we get back all captures -- with $1 and $2 being set to the last two, what we then get in each for-loop iteration. But the while loop sets the scalar context for its condition and then /g iterates through matches in the string so each time we get back the next pair of the specified two captures, with the corresponding $1 and $2.

  • The -Mv5.14 is there for say, as the simple -E isn't good for future. Thanks to ikegami

  • That \d is Unicode and locale aware and it matches anything that has \p{Digit} property. That's some 300-odd characters I think from various writing systems and this can be very misleading or even dangerous, if you cross paths with Unicode.

    This is constrained to ASCII by the /a modifier but why not use [0-9] if you want ASCII?

    See perlrecharclass and for instance this SO page. Also, ask AI for examples, like: perl show examples of what kinds of unicode characters the \d pattern for a digit matches in a regex
